passage:
Dear Professor Usha,
Thank you for your comments on my thesis proposal. I understand you think the second topic, on water pricing in small towns, has better data and a clearer method. I agree it's probably stronger on paper. But I'd really like to continue with my first draft on street-vendor apps. I've spent a lot of time on it, and honestly it feels like mine in a way the new topic doesn't. I know you said the data is thin, and that two seniors dropped similar ideas. Still, I think if I work harder, the draft can get there. Could we meet on Thursday so I can explain why it's worth more than it looks?
Regards,
Vishal

qa.q: What is the second topic, which Professor Usha preferred, about?
qa.a: The second topic is about water pricing in small towns.

qa.q: Why does Vishal want to keep the first draft after agreeing the second topic is stronger?
qa.a: Vishal feels attached and protective toward the first draft because, after so much time spent on it, it feels like Vishal's own. So it seems worth more than it is, even with thin data.

qa.q: What question could Vishal ask before Thursday's meeting?
qa.a: Vishal could ask: if both topics were brand new today, which would I pick? That strips away the extra value the draft gets just from being mine.

qa.q: How might Professor Usha read this email?
qa.a: The professor may notice that the only reason given is that the draft feels like Vishal's, and prepare to gently compare both topics on data and method.

grounding: Shows a student refusing to drop a first draft because it feels like the student's own, valuing it above a better alternative.

passage: Avni, before you say anything, yes, I know the scooter is old. I'm Kashish, and that red scooter has carried me through three years of college. The mechanic says it's worth maybe eighteen thousand. Eighteen! I told the buyer who came yesterday I won't take less than forty. He laughed and left. Everyone keeps saying a new electric one would save me money every month and I'd stop pushing this one up the hostel slope. But this one knows me. The dent on the side is from my first fall. Would I pay forty thousand for someone else's old scooter with a dent? Obviously not. That's different, though. This one is mine.

qa.q: What is the scooter worth, according to the mechanic?
qa.a: The mechanic says it's worth maybe eighteen thousand.

qa.q: Why does Kashish ask forty thousand when the mechanic says eighteen?
qa.a: Kashish feels fond of and protective about the scooter because it holds three years of memories, like the dent from the first fall. So it seems worth far more than the market says.

qa.q: What could Kashish do with the question already asked out loud?
qa.a: Kashish could take "would I pay forty for someone else's?" seriously and price the scooter as a buyer would, keeping the memories in photos rather than in a high price.

qa.q: How might the buyer who laughed see Kashish's price?
qa.a: The buyer likely saw forty thousand as unrealistic for an old dented scooter and felt there was no point in bargaining.

grounding: Shows a student refusing to sell an old scooter at market value because of owning it, pricing it far above what buyers pay.

passage: I'm Simran, and I'm in Tarun's design studio group. For our final project, he made the first concept for the bus shelter: a curved roof like a leaf. Everyone liked it at first. Then Rekha ma'am showed us a second concept from another member: simpler, cheaper, and better at keeping rain out. Even Tarun admitted the leaf roof leaked in the model. But he wouldn't let it go. "I've built three models of this," he said. "It's mine. It's more original." He spent the whole weekend fixing leaks instead of helping with the new one. I don't know if he really thinks it's better or just can't give it up.

qa.q: What shape was Tarun's first concept roof?
qa.a: It was a curved roof like a leaf.

qa.q: Why does Tarun keep fixing the leaf roof after admitting it leaks?
qa.a: Tarun feels attached and protective of the leaf roof because he built three models and it is his idea. So it feels more valuable to him than the simpler design, even though the other one works better.

qa.q: What could the group suggest to help Tarun compare fairly?
qa.a: They could score both concepts on cost, rain and build time without names on them, so ownership doesn't tip the scale.

qa.q: How might the member whose concept was chosen feel about Tarun's weekend?
qa.a: That member may feel frustrated or ignored, since the better design needed help that went into fixing leaks instead.

grounding: Shows a student clinging to his own first design over a better alternative because it is his, as seen by a groupmate.

passage:
Monday. Sahil, twenty, had written the first draft of the college magazine's cover story: a long, dreamy piece about the canteen's history. Keerthana, the editor, read it and said, "Nice, but the students' strike about canteen prices is the real story. Could you rework it around that?" Sahil held the pages tight. "This one's mine. I wrote it at 2 a.m. It's good."
Wednesday. Keerthana showed him the new angle drafted by another writer, sharper and more urgent. Sahil read it and felt a small drop in his stomach. He still thought his draft was better, but he couldn't say why, except that it was his.
Friday. He sat with both pieces at the library. He asked himself: if both were written by strangers, which would I pick? The strike piece. Clearly. He walked to Keerthana's desk. "Use the strike angle. Maybe my history bit can be a side box." She grinned. "Deal."

qa.q: What was Sahil's first draft about?
qa.a: A long, dreamy piece about the canteen's history.

qa.q: Why did Sahil feel his draft was better even when he couldn't say why?
qa.a: Because he wrote it, at 2 a.m., it felt more valuable to him than any other version. His ownership made the draft seem better than it was.

qa.q: What question did Sahil ask himself on Friday, and what did it lead to?
qa.a: Which piece he'd pick if strangers had written both. The honest answer, the strike piece, led him to suggest using it with his history as a side box.

qa.q: How might Keerthana have felt when Sahil walked up to her desk on Friday?
qa.a: Keerthana was probably relieved and pleased, having waited patiently for Sahil to see it himself.

grounding: A student clings to his own first draft over a clearly better angle until he asks which he would choose if strangers wrote both.

passage: Sonali, your chacha has a confession. When I was twenty, I had an old guitar with a cracked neck. I'd bought it second-hand at sixteen and learned every song on it. In my final year I needed a laptop, and I decided to sell the guitar. I put it up for eight thousand. The music shop offered two. A friend offered two and a half. I was outraged. "Do you know how many songs I've played on this?" I kept it listed for four months. Meanwhile I wrote my project reports in the cyber café, paying by the hour. One day my roommate asked, "Saurabh, if you saw this guitar in a shop for eight thousand, would you buy it?" I laughed. Of course not. The neck was cracked. That was the day I understood it was worth eight thousand only to me. I sold it the next week.

qa.q: How much did the music shop offer for the guitar?
qa.a: The music shop offered two.

qa.q: Why was Saurabh outraged by the offers?
qa.a: The guitar held years of songs and memories for him, so it felt worth far more than its market price. Owning it made it feel special.

qa.q: What question from the roommate was the turning point?
qa.a: "If you saw this guitar in a shop for eight thousand, would you buy it?" It made Saurabh see the guitar the way a buyer would.

qa.q: How might Sonali feel hearing that Saurabh chacha kept a cracked guitar listed for four months?
qa.a: Sonali might find it funny and touching, and it could help Sonali notice when something feels precious just because it is owned. 😊

grounding: An uncle tells Sonali how at twenty he refused to sell his old guitar at the market price because it was his.
